label: thm:white_classification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:white_classification}
    Let \(M_0\subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) an embedded, closed, smooth, mean convex hypersurface, and let \(\{M_t\}\) be the corresponding mean curvature flow. If \(X = (x_0,t_0)\) is a singular point, then each tangent flow at \(X\) is a shrinking sphere or cylinder. In other words, if \(\tilde{M}_t\) is a tangent flow to \(M_t\) at \(X\), then \(\tilde{M}_{-1}\) is (up to rotation) of the form \(\mathbb{R}^k\times \mathbb{S}^{n-k}\) for some \(k\in \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}\).
head: environment

label: rem:mean_convex_limit
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:mean_convex_limit}
    First note that if \(U\) is mean convex then the inner and outer flows coincide and \(F_t(U) = \overline{\bigcup_j F_t(U^j)}\) \cite[Section 3]{Altsh95}. Using in addition that \(F_t(U^j)\uparrow F_t(U)\) as discussed above, a standard topological argument implies that \(\partial F_t(U^j)\) converges to \(\partial F_t(U)\) in the Hausdorff sense. If we additionally take our inner approximation \(U^j\) to be mean convex, then the non-fattening result above tells us that \(F_t(\partial U^j)\to F_t(\partial U)\) in the Hausdorff sense.
head: environment

label: prop:graphicality
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:graphicality}
    Suppose that \(M_0\) satisfies hypothesis (H1) or (H2), and let \(\{M_t\}_{t< t_0}\) be the corresponding smooth mean curvature flow. Up to the first singular time \(t_0\), \(M_t\) remains a smooth \(SO(p)\times SO(q)\)-invariant hypersurface generated by some \(u_t\in C^0([\xi_1(t),\xi_2(t)])\cap C^\infty((\xi_1(t),x_2(t)))\) or \(u_t\in C^0([0,\xi_2(t)])\cap C^\infty((0,x_2(t)))\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Due to the preservation of \(SO(p)	imes SO(q)\) symmetry, the mean curvature flow \(\{M_t\}\) can be described by the evolution of a 1-parameter family of profile curves \(\gamma(\cdot,t)\). If we can rule out vertical tangents (i.e. tangents parallel to \(\mathbf{e}_{p+1}\)) from forming at any time up to the singular time and away from \(P_1\), then the desired result follows from the implicit function theorem. Let \(
u\) be the outward normal to \(M_t\). Its restriction to \(P_0\) induces a normal on \(\gamma\) which we denote by \(	ilde{
u}\). Vertical tangents occur precisely when \(	ilde{
u}\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1} = 0\). To rule this out, it suffices to show that \(
u \cdot\mathbf{e}_{p+1}>0\) on \(\hat{M}_t  ackslash \partial \hat{M}_t\), where \(\hat{M}_t \coloneqq M_t\cap \{y_1>0\}\), as this then implies that \(	ilde{
u}\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1}>0\) as well. Our assumptions on \(M_0\) give that \(
u\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1}\geq 0\) on \(\hat{M}_0\), with equality holding on \(\partial \hat{M}_0\) only. The smoothness of the flow up to the first singular time implies that \(
u\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1} \geq 0\) for \(0\leq t< t_0\). Now, using that \(
u\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1}\) satisfies \((\partial_t - \Delta)(
u\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1}) = |A|^2(
u\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1})\), it follows from the weak maximum principle that \(
u\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1} \geq 0\) on \(\hat{M}_t\), and by the strong maximum principle that \(
u\cdot \mathbf{e}_{p+1} > 0\) on \(\hat{M}_t ackslash \partial \hat{M}_t\).

label: rem:curvilinear
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:curvilinear}
    It is possible to apply Theorem \ref{thm:sturmian_theorem} on a non-rectangular domain, as is done in Section 2.1 of \cite{Coicu24}. Specifically, it is possible to replace \(\{x_1,x_2\}\times(0,t_0]\) with \(\{x_1(t),x_2(t)\}\times(0,t_0]\), where \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are analytic in \(t\), and \(u(x_j(t),t)\neq v(x_j(t),t)\) for \(0\leq t<t_0\).

label: prop:bubblesheet
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bubblesheet}
    Suppose that \(M_0 = \Sigma_u\) is mean convex, satisfies hypothesis (H1) or (H2) and the corresponding level set flow \(\{M_t\}_{t>0}\) does not vanish at the first singular time \(t_0\). Suppose further that \(X_0 = (x_0,t_0)\) is a singular point with \(x_0\in P_0\). Then \(x_0\) must lie on \(P_1\) but not at a \(P_1\)-crossing point of \(M_{t_0}\). Moreover, the tangent flow at \(X_0\) is a shrinking \( \mathbb{R}^2\times \mathbb{S}^1\), with the \(\mathbb{S}^1\) factor parallel to \(P_2\).
head: environment

label: lem:disc_containment
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The argument in each case follows the same approach. Therefore, we prove (a) in full detail, then point out relevant modifications for the remaining parts.
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item By its rotational symmetry around \(P_2\), \(M_{t_0}\) contains a circle \(C\) of radius \(x^*>0\)  centred at \((0,0,y^*,0)\) and parallel to \(P_1\). Let \(\tilde{C}^k = \{s_k(x-x_0):x\in C\}\), then by mean convexity of the flow, it follows that \(\tilde{C}^k\subset \tilde{M}_t^k\) for all \(t< t_0\). Note that \(\tilde{C}^k\) is a circle of radius \(s_kx^*\) with one point passing through the origin and all other points having negative \(x_1\)-coordinate. It follows that \(\tilde{C}^k\to \ell\) in a local smooth sense. As containment is preserved by local smooth convergence, it follows that \(\ell\subset \tilde{M}_t\). 
        \item Since \(M_t\) is generated by a graphical profile curve up to the singular time, it follows that the interior of \(M_{t_0}\) contains the disc \(D_1\) of radius \(y^*>0\) centred at \((x^*,0,0,0)\) and parallel to \(P_2\). The argument follows as before.
        \item 
        \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
            \item If the hypersurface crosses \(P_2\), we apply the same argument as before with the disc \(D_2\) of radius \(x^*>0\) centred at 0 and lying in \(P_1\). If the hypersurface avoids \(P_2\), we apply this argument with the disc \(D_3\) lying in \(P_1\) and touching \(M_{t_0}\) only at the left \(P_1\)-crossing point and at \(x_0\).  
            \item  We apply the same argument as before to the disc \(D_4\) which touches \(M_{t_0}\) at the left and right \(P_1\)-crossing points. \qedhere
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lem:away_from_axes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:away_from_axes}
    Suppose \(M_0\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition \ref{prop:bubblesheet} and \(X_0 = (x_0,t_0)\) is a singular point with \(x_0\in P_0\). Then \(x_0\) must lie on \(P_1\) or \(P_2\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose for a contradiction that \(x_0\) is of the form \((x^*,0,y^*,0)\) with \(x^*\neq 0\) and \(y^*\neq 0\). By statements (a) and (b) of Lemma \ref{lem:disc_containment}, the tangent flow \(\tilde{M}_t\) at \(X_0\) must contain \(\ell \subset P_1\) and \(H_2^-\subset P_2\). Since \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are orthogonal, it follows that \(\tilde{M}_t\) contains \(\ell\times H_2^- = \{(\bar{x},\bar{y})\in \mathbb{R}^4:x_1 = 0,y_1\leq 0\}\) in its interior. However, we also know that \(\tilde{M}_t\) must be a shrinking \(\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{S}^2\) or \(\mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{S}^1\), neither of which contain \(\ell\times H_2^-\). This contradicts that \(X_0\) is a singular point.
head: environment

label: lem:away_from_endpoints
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:away_from_endpoints}
    Suppose \(M_0\) satisfies the conditions of Proposition \ref{prop:bubblesheet} and \(X_0 = (x_0,t_0)\) is a singular point with \(x_0\in P_0\). Then \(x_0\) cannot lie at any crossing point of \(M_{t_0}\), except the origin.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We show this only in the case of a right \(P_1\)-crossing point of \(M_{t_0}\). The proofs in the case of a \(P_2\)-crossing point and a left \(P_1\)-crossing point are analogous (using (b) and (c)(ii) of Lemma \ref{lem:disc_containment} respectively instead of (c)(i)).

    Suppose \(x_0 = (x^*,0,0,0)\) lies at a right \(P_1\)-crossing point (so \(x^*\neq 0\)). Up to the first singular time, the outward normal vector to the surface at \(x_0\) points in the \(\mathbf{e}_1\) direction, so the tangent vector to the profile curve points in the \(\mathbf{e}_3\) direction, and this property is preserved by the local smooth convergence when we extract a tangent flow at \(X_0\). Therefore, parabolic rescaling of the profile curve gives a copy of \(\{(\bar{x},\bar{y})\in \mathbb{R}^4: x_1=0\}\) in \(P_0\). By the rotational symmetry around \(P_1\) (which is preserved by the rescaling), rotation of this line gives all of \(P_2\), so if \(X_0\) is singular, then its tangent flow must be a shrinking \(\mathbb{R}^2\times \mathbb{S}^1\), with the \(\mathbb{S}^1\) factor orthogonal to \(P_2\), i.e. in \(P_1\). However, statement (c)(i) of Lemma \ref{lem:disc_containment} implies that the tangent flow at \(X_0\) contains \(H_1^-\), which cannot be contained in \(\mathbb{S}^1\). This is a contradiction.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemmas \ref{lem:away_from_axes} and \ref{lem:away_from_endpoints} immediately imply \(x_0\) lies on \(P_1\), but cannot be a \(P_1\)-crossing point. This proves the first claim. Let us now turn to the second claim, that the tangent flow at \(X_0\) is \(\mathbb{R}^2\times \mathbb{S}^1\) with \(\mathbb{S}^1\subset P_2\). We split our proof of this claim into the cases \(x_0\neq 0\) and \(x_0 = 0\).

    If \(x_0\neq 0\), then in the plane \(P_2\), the translated flow \(M_t-x_0\) consists of concentric circles centred at 0 of radius \(r(t)\), where \(r(t)\to 0\) as \(t\to t_0\). Consequently, the \(\tilde{M}_t^k\cap P_2\) consists of concentric circles of radius \(s_kr(s_k^{-2}t+t_0)\), still centred at \(0\). By the avoidance principle it follows that
    \begin{align*}
        \operatorname{dist}\left(M_{s_k^{-2}t+t_0},x_0\right) \leq \sqrt{6s_k^{-2}t}.
    \end{align*}
    In particular \(s_kr(s_k^{-2}t+t_0)\leq \sqrt{6t}\), so the rescaled radii are uniformly bounded for each \(t\). It follows that there exits \(r^*(t)\) for which \(s_kr(s_k^{-2}t+t_0)\to r^*(t)\). Therefore, the intersection of the tangent flow with \(P_2\) contains a copy of \(\mathbb{S}^1\). By our previous discussion, the tangent flow at \(X_0\) must be a shrinking \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^2\) or \(\mathbb{R}^2\times\mathbb{S}^1\). Since we are working in the case where \(x^*>0\), and we ruled out \(x_0\) being a left \(P_1\)-crossing point in the first half of the proposition, we can apply statement (c)(i) of Lemma \ref{lem:disc_containment} to conclude that the tangent flow at \(x_0\) contains \(H_1^-\). This cannot be contained in the interior of \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^2\), so our tangent flow must be a shrinking \(\mathbb{R}^2\times\mathbb{S}^1\).

    If \(x_0=0\), then by the same proof as above, the intersection of our tangent flow with \(P_2\) is a copy of \(\mathbb{S}^1\), so the tangent flow at \(X_0\) must either be a shrinking \(\mathbb{R}^2\times\mathbb{S}^1\) or \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^2\). Assume for a contradiction that it is a shrinking \(\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{S}^2\). Since the intersection of the tangent flow with \(P_2\) contains \(\mathbb{S}^1\), the Euclidean factor must be perpendicular to \(P_2\). But then, by the rotational symmetry around \(P_2\) (which is preserved since there is no translation in this case), it follows that \(\mathbb{R}^2\) must be contained in the interior of \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{S}^2\), which is a contradiction.

label: lem:singularities_are_flat
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:singularities_are_flat}
    Suppose \(M_0 = \Sigma_u\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition \ref{prop:bubblesheet}, and let \(\xi\) be such that \(u(\xi,t_0) = 0\), excluding the endpoints \(\xi_1(t_0)\) and \(\xi_2(t_0)\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\mu_\varepsilon\) such that \(u(x,t_0)\leq \varepsilon |x-\xi|\) for \(|x-\xi|\leq \mu_\varepsilon\).

label: lem:continuity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:continuity}
    Suppose \(M_0= \Sigma_u\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition \ref{prop:bubblesheet}, then \(u(\cdot,t_0)\) is a continuous function that is smooth away from its zero set \(Z_{t_0} = \{\xi:u(\xi,t_0) = 0 \}\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show smoothness. We know from Proposition \ref{prop:bubblesheet} that \(M_{t_0}\) is smooth away from \(P_1\), so we can apply the strong maximum principle to \(\nu\cdot \mathbf{e}_3\) to conclude that the corresponding profile curve has no vertical tangents, as in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:graphicality}. Away from \(P_1\), this profile curve can be represented as a smooth graph over the \(x_1\)-axis by the implicit function theorem, which must correspond to the graph of \(u(\cdot, t_0)\) by uniqueness. 

    Continuity at the end-points follows from the fact that, in a neighbourhood of each end-point, the profile curve admits a smooth graphical representation over the \(y_1\)-axis. The image of this graph must agree with the representation of the curve as a graph over the \(x_1\)-axis in some overlapping region, and therefore determines the same limit at the end-point, ensuring continuity there. Finally, for any point \(\xi\in Z_{t_0}\) that is not an end-point, it follows from Lemma \ref{lem:singularities_are_flat} that \(\lim_{x\to\xi} u(x,t_0) = 0\). Since \(u(\xi,t_0) = 0\), continuity follows.

label: lem:hyperboloid_comparison
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider \(f(\bar{x},\bar{y},t) = y_1^2 + y_2^2 - (1-\beta)(x_1^2 + x_2^2) + \beta t\) for some \(0\leq \beta \leq 1\), then
    \begin{align*}
        \left(\frac{d}{dt} - \Delta_{M_t}\right)f(\bar{x},\bar{y},t)
        &= \left(\frac{d}{dt} - \Delta_{M_t}\right)\left(|(\bar{x},\bar{y})|^2 - x_1^2 - x_2^2 - (1-\beta)(x_1^2 + x_2^2) + \beta t\right)\\
        &= -6 + 2(2-\beta)(|\nabla^{M_t}x_1|^2 + |\nabla^{M_t}x_2|^2) + \beta
        \leq 2-3\beta,
    \end{align*}
    and this is non-positive when \(\beta \geq 2/3\). The first claim now follows from the weak maximum principle. For the second claim, note that since the initial surface is diffeomorphic to \(\mathbb{S}^3\) and topological changes can only occur at singular times, it follows that \(M_t\cong \mathbb{S}^3\) up to the first singular time. If no singularity has formed before time \(\varepsilon^2/\beta\), then \(M_t\) must still cross \(P_2\) at this time, but is also forced by the barrier to lie inside a cone with vertex at the origin, which is not possible if \(M_t\cong \mathbb{S}^3\). Therefore a singularity has to have formed before this time.
head: environment

label: prop:non_vanishing
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First note that the condition \(g<u<h\) implies that upon rotation
    \begin{align*}
        B_\rho((p\cos\psi,p\sin\psi,0,0))
        \subset M_0
        \subset \{(\bar{x},\bar{y})\in \mathbb{R}^4:(1-\beta)(x_1^2 + x_2^2) \geq y_1^2 + y_2^2 - \varepsilon^2\},
    \end{align*}
    for any \(\psi \in [0,2\pi)\). Therefore, \(M_0\) satisfies the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lem:hyperboloid_comparison}, and a singularity forms at the latest time of \(\varepsilon^2/\beta\). Now, take any \(\rho^2 > {6\varepsilon^2}/{\beta}\) and suppose that \(M_t\) has vanished at time \({\varepsilon^2}/{\beta}\). Since \(B_\rho((p\cos\psi,p\sin\psi,0,0))\subset M_0\), it follows from the avoidance principle that \(B_{\sqrt{\rho^2-6\varepsilon^2/\beta}}((p\cos\psi,p\sin\psi,0,0)) \subset M_{\varepsilon^2/\beta}\),
    and the radius of the ball on the left hand side is strictly positive by our choice of \(\rho\). However, by assumption, \(M_{\varepsilon^2/\beta}\) has vanished, and therefore cannot contain a 4-ball in its interior. So we have a contradiction.

label: prop:singularity_at_origin
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:singularity_at_origin}
    Suppose that \(M_0 = \Sigma_u\) is mean convex and that there exists \(0<p<\xi_2\), such that \(u_{x}(\cdot,0)>0\) on \((0,p)\) and  \(u_{x}(\cdot,0)<0\) on \((p,\xi_2]\), and \(u_x(0,0) = u_x(p,0) = 0\). Then there exists \(\varepsilon_0\) such that if \(M_0\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition \ref{prop:non_vanishing} with \(\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\), then for all \(t<t_0\), there exists \(p(t)\) such that \(u_{x}(\cdot,t)>0\) on \((0,p(t))\) and \(u_x(\cdot,0) < 0\) on \((p(t),\xi_2]\).

label: cor:singularity_connected
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:singularity_connected}
    Suppose that \(M_0= \Sigma_u\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition \ref{prop:singularity_at_origin}, then the zero set \(Z_{t_0} = \{\xi\in [0,\xi_2(t_0)]:u(\xi,t) = 0\}\) is of the form \([0,\eta]\cup \{\xi_2(t_0)\}\) for some \(\eta < \xi_2(t_0)\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By the continuity of \(u(\cdot,t_0)\) (c.f. Lemma \ref{lem:continuity}) it follows that \(Z_{t_0}\) is closed. Moreover, the zero at \(\xi_2(t_0)\) is isolated due to the fact that the gradient of \(u(\cdot,t_0)\) approaches \(-\infty\) near \(\xi_2(t_0)\). Suppose for a contradiction that \(Z_{t_0}\backslash \{\xi(t_0)\}\) has multiple connected components, then between each of then there will be a point at which \(u(\cdot,t_0)\) attains a positive value. Applying the mean value theorem and considering the flow slightly back in time, one finds that the presence of such a point is not compatible with the shape of the profile curve up to the first singular time given by Proposition \ref{prop:singularity_at_origin}.

label: def:alpha_invertible
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:alpha_invertible}
    Suppose \(\Sigma_u\) satisfies hypothesis (H1), and fix \(\alpha>0\). We say that \(u\) is \emph{\(\alpha\)-invertible} if \(u = \rho\) at exactly two points for each \(0<\rho\leq \alpha\) and \(u_x\neq 0\) at these points.
head: environment

label: lem:alpha_invertible
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:alpha_invertible}
    Suppose \(M_0 = \Sigma_u\) is generated by an \(\alpha\)-invertible function \(u\), and suppose that the corresponding mean curvature flow has first singular time \(t_0\). Then there exists \(t_\alpha\in (0,t_0]\) such that \(u(\cdot,t)\) is \(\alpha(t)\)-invertible for \(0<t<t_\alpha\), where \(\alpha(t) = \sqrt{\alpha^2-2t}\). Moreover, if \(\tilde{u}\geq u\) is another \(\alpha\)-domain satisfying the same assumptions as \(u\) and with first singular time \(\tilde{t}_0\), then \(\tilde{u}(\cdot,t)\) is \(\alpha(t)\)-invertible for \(0<t<t_\alpha\), where \(t_\alpha\) is as before.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(u> \alpha\) away from its endpoints, for small enough \(\varepsilon>0\) we can place a ball of radius \(\varepsilon\) between \(\Sigma_u\) and \(\Sigma_\alpha\). Now take \(t_\alpha = \min \{\varepsilon^2/6, \ \alpha^2/2\}\). If \(\tilde{u}\geq u\), then the same ball will be contained between \(\Sigma_{\tilde{u}}\) and \(\Sigma_\alpha\), so the following arguments hold in this case as well.
    
    We first show that \(u(\cdot,t)\) is \(\alpha(t)\)-invertible for \(t\leq  \min \{t_0,t_\alpha\}\). Given any \(t' < \min \{t_0,t_\alpha\}\), consider some \(0< \rho \leq \alpha(t')\), and define \(\rho(t) = \sqrt{\rho^2 - 2(t-t')}\), so that \(\rho(0) = \sqrt{\rho^2 + 2t'}\leq \alpha\) and \(\rho(t') = \rho\). Due to the spherical barrier, we must have \(u(\cdot,t') = \rho(t')\) at least twice. On the other hand, since \(u(\cdot,0)\) is equal to \(\rho\) twice for all \(\rho< \alpha\), it follows from the Sturmian theorem \ref{thm:sturmian_theorem} (and Remark \ref{rem:curvilinear} to deal with the end-points), that \(u(\cdot,t')\) is equal to \(\rho(t')\) at most twice. Therefore they are equal at exactly two points, and since there was no decrease in the number of zeros of \(u(\cdot,t) - \rho(t)\), the zeros must all be of order 1, so \(u_x(\cdot,t')>0\) at these points. 

    Finally, we want to show that \(t_\alpha \leq t_0\). Suppose not, then \(\Sigma_{u_t}\) becomes singular before \(u(\cdot,t)\) ceases to be \(\alpha(t)\)-invertible. The spherical barrier means that \(\Sigma_{u_t}\) cannot vanish at its first singular time \(t_0\) (since this time is less than \(t_\alpha \leq \varepsilon^2/6\) by assumption). Additionally, since \(\Sigma_u\) is mean convex, Proposition \ref{prop:bubblesheet} tells us that the singularity can only form when \(u=0\), but not at \(\xi_1(t_0)\) and \(\xi_2(t_0)\). However, for each \(t<t_0\), \(u(t)\) is \(\alpha(t)\)-invertible with \(\alpha(t)\geq \alpha(t_0) > \alpha(t_\alpha) \geq 0\), and so we can't have \(u = 0\) away from an end-point. Thus we must have \(t_0\leq t_\alpha\).

label: prop:uniform_derivative_bounds
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:uniform_derivative_bounds}
    Let \(\Sigma_{u^*}\) be as before, and let \(\Sigma_{u^j}\) be the mean convex approximation given by Lemma \ref{lem:mean_convex_approximation}. Then there exists \(T\) such that for any \(\delta \in (0,T)\), the second fundamental form of \(F_t(\Sigma_{u^j})\) and its derivatives are uniformly bounded for \(j\geq 1\) and \(\delta < t < T\).

label: prop:instant_smoothness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:instant_smoothness}
    There is a \(T>0\) such that \(F_t(\Sigma_{u^*})\) is a smooth hypersurface for \(0<t<T\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma \ref{lem:mean_convex_approximation}, \(\Sigma_{u^*}\) admits a mean convex approximation \(\Sigma_{u^j}\). It thus follows from Remark \ref{rem:mean_convex_limit} that \(F_t(\Sigma_{u^j}) \to F_t(\Sigma_{u^*})\) in the Hausdorff sense. On the other hand, Proposition \ref{prop:uniform_derivative_bounds} implies that that \(F_t(\Sigma_{u^j})\) converges uniformly to a smooth hypersurface for \(t\in(0,T)\), therefore by uniqueness of the level set flow the limits must agree and \(F_t(\Sigma_{u^*})\) is smooth.

title: Proof
body_md: We already established statement (1) in Section \ref{sec:topological_change_example}. Now let \(\Sigma_{u^*}\) be as before. By Proposition \ref{prop:instant_smoothness}, there exists \(T>0\) such that \(F_{t}(\Sigma_{u^*})\) is smooth for \(0<t<T\). Since \( F_{t}(\Sigma_{u^*})\) is smooth, closed and avoids \(P_2\) (by mean convexity of the flow), it is a smooth embedding of \(\mathbb{S}^1\times\mathbb{S}^2\). This completes the proof of statement (2).
